title: GlobalFoundries to Manufacture India's First Homegrown RF Chips Designed by Startup Fermionic
excerpt: The commercial partnership marks a milestone for India's semiconductor ambitions, putting a Bangalore startup's radar and satellite communication chips on the same production line as Qualcomm and MediaTek.
body:
• GlobalFoundries will manufacture radio frequency chips designed by Indian startup Fermionic, the first Indian semiconductors the foundry giant has agreed to produce.
  • Fermionic is developing chips for radar, satellite communications and telecom infrastructure under India's Design Linked Incentive scheme.
  • The partnership moves Fermionic from prototype to production-grade silicon, competing alongside Qualcomm, MediaTek and Broadcom on GlobalFoundries' fab lines.
  • India's semiconductor market is projected to reach $150 billion by 2030, and the deal signals growing global confidence in Indian chip design capabilities.

A First for Indian Chip Design

GlobalFoundries Engineering Private Limited and Fermionic, a Bangalore-based fabless semiconductor startup, have announced a commercial partnership under which GlobalFoundries will manufacture Fermionic's radio frequency chips. The deal represents the first time an Indian company's semiconductor designs will be produced by GlobalFoundries, which counts Qualcomm, MediaTek and Broadcom among its manufacturing clients.

The partnership is a concrete milestone for India's long-stated ambition to build a domestic semiconductor ecosystem. While India has established itself as a global hub for chip design services through companies like Synopsys and Cadence, the country has struggled to move from services to products. Fermionic's deal with GlobalFoundries bridges that gap, putting Indian-designed silicon on a path to commercial production.

"Our collaboration with GlobalFoundries India enables us to deliver complex, production-grade RF silicon, not just prototypes, and build the confidence required by our customers in strategic applications."

— Gautam Kumar Singh, CEO, Fermionic

"India's chip market is projected to grow from $33 billion in 2023 to $150 billion by 2030."

"India's chip market is projected to grow from $33 billion in 2023 to $150 billion by 2030."

What Fermionic Is Building

Founded in June 2020 by Gautam Kumar Singh and Prasun Kali Bhattacharyya, Fermionic specializes in high-performance RF and millimeter-wave chips. Its product roadmap includes beamformers, phased-array transceivers, RF switches, high-linearity power amplifier chains and integrated front-end ICs designed for intelligent sensing, adaptive communications and AI-enabled RF systems.

The applications span defense and civilian uses: radar systems, satellite communication networks, telecom infrastructure and next-generation wireless technologies. Many of these are areas where India currently depends on imported components, making domestic production a strategic priority.

Fermionic is part of an early cohort of companies supported under the Indian government's Design Linked Incentive scheme, which provides financial support to fabless chip companies. The startup has also participated in Qualcomm's Semiconductor Mentorship Program and previously raised $6 million in its first external funding round.

Why This Partnership Matters

For Fermionic, the deal solves a critical challenge facing Indian chip startups: moving from lab designs to production-ready silicon. RF chip manufacturing requires specialized expertise, and finding a foundry partner willing to work with a young startup on complex analog designs is no small feat.

Singh emphasized that Fermionic needed "more than a manufacturing vendor" and sought "a partner who understands RF complexity and can support production-grade execution." GlobalFoundries' RF expertise and its India engineering team provided that match.

For the broader Indian semiconductor ecosystem, the deal is a proof point. India's chip market is projected to grow from $33 billion in 2023 to $150 billion by 2030. The government has committed over ₹76,000 crore to incentive programs supporting semiconductor development. But turning those investments into commercially viable products requires partnerships like this one.

What's Next

Fermionic currently operates with a team of about 35 engineers and plans to expand to 60–70 in the coming year, adding system engineering and application engineering capabilities. The company expects its RF components to enter full-volume production soon, initially targeting radar and satellite communication customers.

Other Indian fabless companies, including Saankhya Labs, Signalchip and Terminus Circuits, are also pushing to commercialize Indian-designed chips. Fermionic's GlobalFoundries deal could open doors for similar partnerships across the sector, demonstrating that Indian chip designs can meet the manufacturing standards of the world's leading foundries.
